deities: Lord Manjunatha Swamy (Shiva linga - presiding deity, brought from Kadri, Mangalore)
Tirthankara Chandranath Swamy (Jain shrine within the complex)
Kalarahu, Kalarkayi, Kumaraswami and Kanyakumari (the four Dharma Daivas, the protective guardian deities)
festivals: Laksha Deepotsava - five-day festival of lights in Kartika (November-December), the grandest annual celebration
Annual Jathre (nine-day festival with car festival, held in April)
Shivarathri (night-long bhajan with special poojas and car festival)
Navarathri (nine days, special worship at the Sri Ammanavaru shrine)
Deepavali (festival of lights and commencement of special annual ceremonies)
Patthanaje (the last festival, held in May before the monsoons)

history.dynasty: Hereditary administration by the Jain Heggade family (Dharmadhikaris); the temple's origins are legendary rather than tied to a ruling dynasty
history.period: Tradition places the origins about 800 years ago; originally called Kuduma; the temple's present fame and institutions are built up under the Heggade family, currently led by Dr. D. Veerendra Heggade
history.summary: Sri Manjunatha Swamy Temple at Dharmasthala is one of Karnataka's most famous pilgrimage centres, with a history of over 800 years. Originally the place was called Kuduma. According to tradition, angels in human form visited the pious Jain householder Barmana Heggade and his family; impressed by their hospitality, they appeared in his dream, promised to stay at Kuduma, and asked him to feed the needy daily. Heggade built shrines for Kalarahu, Kalarkai, Kumarswamy and Kanyakumari, the Dharma Daivas. Later, Annappa Swamy, the messenger of the daivas, brought a Shivalinga from Kadri in Mangalore, and Heggade built the Manjunatha Swamy temple and installed it; Kuduma then became Dharmasthala - 'the place where Dharma is a way of life'. The temple is uniquely administered by the Jain Heggade family (Dharmadhikaris) while the priests are Madhva (Vaishnavite) Brahmins, and it houses both Hindu and Jain shrines - the tirthankara Chandraprabha (Chandranath Swamy basadi) alongside Shaivite and the four Dharma Daivas. The famous free mass-feeding (Annadana) at the Annapurna dining hall continues to this day. The town also has educational institutions, a museum and the Manjusha vintage car museum.

name: Sri Manjunatha Swamy Temple
town: Dharmasthala (CSV town 'Dharmasthala' is correct; town is in Belthangadi taluk)
town_description: Dharmasthala is a famous temple town in Belthangadi taluk of Dakshina Kannada district, Karnataka, about 75 km from Mangalore. Built around the 800-year-old Sri Manjunatha Swamy temple and uniquely administered by the Jain Heggade family, it is known for its free mass feeding (Annadana), the Laksha Deepotsava festival, its educational institutions, the Manjusha museum and car museum, and the nearby 39-ft Bahubali statue on Ratnagiri hill.
tradition: Hinduism (Shaivism) - with strong Jain elements: administered by a Jain Dharmadhikari family and housing a Jain basadi; priests are Vaishnavite (Madhva) Brahmins

travel.road: Well connected by road; frequent KSRTC buses run from Mangalore (~75 km), Bengaluru and other Karnataka cities; the temple address is Sri Kshetra Dharmasthala, Dakshina Kannada 574216.

visitor_information.best_time: October to March is the best time to visit (winter/pleasant season); the Laksha Deepotsava in November-December is the grandest but most crowded. Avoid the heavy monsoon season (June-September).
visitor_information.opening_hours: Darshan roughly 6:30 AM - 2:30 PM and 5:00 PM - 8:30 PM daily (sources vary slightly - verify). Daily routine includes Shatarudra Abhisheka 8:30-10:30 AM, Mahapooja 12:00 noon and 8:30 PM; devotee darshan is blocked during Mahapooja and Nithyabali. Free Annadana (lunch) is served at the Annapurna dining hall; paid special darshan queue (about Rs 200) is available.
